projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Daniel Ash was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: All right. When you answer me or when I ask, you know, you'll say "my name is." And, then, just say your name, when you were born, where you were born, you know, what your family did, how you grew up and that kind of stuff.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Okay. Well, my name is Daniel David Ash. I say both names because part of my family knows me as David. During service time, I'm known as Daniel. And I was born down in Greenwood, around Greenwood, Delaware, and I was raised around Bridgeville. And when I was in the tenth grade, I was going to school in Milton, and that's when I was drafted out of school into the service.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did your family do?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, my parents were farmers. My father was a farmer. And that was, of course, it was back during the depression. And it was a good thing to be on the farm because if you were poor, you had some kind of source to get the food.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Let's talk about -- tell me, you were born in Greenboro?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Greenwood.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I mean Greenwood.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Greenwood.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Greenwood. And what was the size of your family? Let's talk about that.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, I'm one of the brothers from 9 children. And I was the only one born in Delaware. The rest of them were born in western Maryland. And I guess that's about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: But you all grew up on the farm -- was there all boys?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, we all grew up on the farm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many boys and how many girls or were they all boys?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, there was eight boys and one girl. My sister was the second one in the family.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, are they all still here? Are they all -- tell me a little bit about that.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And where did you fall in line?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: I'm the youngest one. I'm always called the baby. And still am. And -- what was the question?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Your family, where are they located?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Okay. We were all raised down around Bridgeville mostly. One of them moved to Pennsylvania. And I ended up in South Carolina for a while. My oldest brother he was the first one that went in the Service. And then another brother went in, and, of course, rotated along. And finally in '45, in '45, March '45, I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: As a, as a sophomore in high school?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: No. I just -- I got in --I got in senior. It was in tenth grade.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tenth grade?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, I missed a few years.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were in tenth grade when you got drafted?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Uh-huh. And that's why I got my diploma last year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Last year?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Really? Tell me a little bit about that.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, the state had decided to award veterans that were drafted out of school a high-school diploma, so I finally got my high-school diploma.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Good. So let's -- so there is a lot of story here. Okay. Let's go back to Pearl Harbor. Do you remember that at all, do you remember when that happened?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, I remember that. I don't really remember where I was when it happened.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You were down in Bridgeville someplace. Did your older brother go? How did that all happen? You were -- Pearl Harbor happened -- say Pearl Harbor happened. Then what happened? Do you remember that? I mean, do you remember who went first, why they went, where they went?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, my brother, my brother Perry went first. He's the oldest. And then Roy, my brother Roy went next. And then Frank and my brother Adam and I were -- took basic training at the same time in Camp Blanding, Florida. And my brother -- well, my brother Minno, he's the only one still living, he was stationed on the West Coast in the artillery battery.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Now, tell me a little bit about, you were going to school. You were in tenth grade. Say "I was going to school, I was in tenth grade," at Milton?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, that was a long story. I just, I just more or less went to school about that time. I was staying with a family down there on the farm. And a, that's about it as far as I know. Wasn't nothing exciting. I didn't take any athletic training or anything like that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Welll, were they doing --

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Hold on a second. (Inaudible) is having a snack.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: A snack. No, I mean, you were in the tenth grade?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: In March?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. But all of a sudden you got your notice?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Notice, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were going to school. You came home, found out that they had drafted you?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me a little bit about that, how that happened. And then you went -- from down there, you got on a bus and you went to Florida?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Jersey, New Jersey, inducted over in New Jersey. I forget the name of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Then?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Then we went from there down to Florida.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So tell me, you were in tenth grade. It was in March. And you were working on the farm?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Going to school. "I was working" -- just tell me, "I was" -- you were working on the farm.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Say that to me. Tell me.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, "I was, I was working on the farm," uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Then "I was working on the farm" and then "I was going to school."

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me that back. "I was working on the farm. I was going to school. And in March they drafted me." 1945?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, I -- I guess I just went to school. Nothing out of the ordinary or anything about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. But you came home and you found out you were gonna go in.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah. But then I found out, I was gonna go in. I was really wanting to go in, but I didn't, didn't have the nerve to go sign up. And my sister was trying to keep me -- put me different places to keep me out. And I was, I was ready to -- I was glad to get drafted, because I wanted to go in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, how old were you? "I was" --

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: 18. I was drafted when I was 18.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. So then you went to Florida.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah. Camp Blanding, Florida.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Took basic training. And I'd say my brother was there -- my brother Adam was there at the same time, not the same company, but different companies. And from there, basic training, I went to Alabama, I forget the camp, but took two days -- two weeks of jungle training, and after that went from -- took troop training to Fort Ord, California. Then we shipped out from there. And that was where we were really got a thrill, about four days out on the ocean on a troop ship, the war was ended. And a -- but we kept going and we were, we were still on alert because we knew there was, we knew there was some submarines still out there that didn't get the word and we might get torpedoed. But we made it on and we went to Philippines. And I was in the Philippines for about two weeks. And after that, we were transferred to, we went to Japan. That's the occupation troop. And that's about the most exciting part about my service is -- was the typhoon as we were going across the ocean. You see --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Waves?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The tor -- the funnels?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: The bombs in the ocean, whatever.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, mines?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Mines, you see mines across on the side that were still there, we went through the middle of them. And afterwards, you could hear gunners shooting getting -- putting them out of commission after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How bad was this ship? Was it an actual troop ship?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: It was an actual troop ship, but due to the waves and all, we just had a, bam, it would just pick the front end up out of the water and slap it back down. And, and I was really fortunate to be in the front.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were in, was it tight quarters? How many people do you think were on it?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How many people -- was it tight quarters and how many troops do you think were aboard?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Oh, I don't know. Well, it was quite a few of us. It was a whole troop ship. And after, well, when I got into Japan, I was attached to the 32nd division, MP unit and we just patrolled the streets and things like that. Like daily, like I said, we didn't have any trouble with them, the people there. The fact is, I made pretty good friends with one family, but I lost, lost her address and I lost touch with them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How long were you in Japan and then when did you come home?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, I was there about six months or so. It was nine months after, after I was inducted. I reenlisted for three years. I got homesick, so I wanted to go home. So I enlisted, got a 30-day leave. And then after that, we come back to the states.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's when you ended up in --

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: That's when I ended up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Ended up being attached out of Fort Jackson?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, no, I spent my three years -- I was signed up for Germany, but I never saw Germany. I was, I was a, went to MP unit in Memphis, Tennessee. And from there, I went to Chattanooga, Tennessee for a month for disciplinary barracks training. And from there I went to Augusta, Georgia, I forget the name, it's a fort now, it's not a camp. But were -- the disciplinary barracks was the only units there. And we just patrolled them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, let's go back to your brothers again. All your brothers, I mean, did you guys write? Did you know where they were? Were any of them wounded? Were they, were they in any of the action? Did you worry about them?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, but we, we never did do too much writing but my, one of my brothers served in Italy. And my oldest brother served in Germany and the Pacific. And my brother Frank served in Germany. And -- well, after training, my brother Adam next to me that was in, he, he went to Germany in the occupation. And when we were in Japan, I didn't know it till I got home, but my oldest brother was in -- was there too up in Tokyo. And I was on the island of Honshu.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you run into any other Delawarians or any people that you knew from Delaware that were over there with you or in your unit or anything?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah. I ran into some but I can't remember who they were. The other day I found my old diary I kept, and there's two in there from Delaware. I tried to contact them but they were both already passed away.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You have a diary of when you were in?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: For a while. Not for the whole thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Through basic training, I had a diary.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. That's what would be interesting to be read. (Talking in whispered tones.)

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah. When you were on that troop ship and you found out that the war was over, now which part was over? Was it Japan?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Japan, it was Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. Tell me about, what were your emotion -- when you found it out, what was everybody -- you guys were probably tense knowing you were going over to it, and now all of a sudden you heard this news?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, there's no doubt about it, we were all happy, but we didn't really show too much emotion, I don't think. We were just, just kind of glad it was over, that's all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Because you were going over there to do a job anyway, so it didn't --

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah, well, I didn't have a job on the troop ship, but coming back from Japan, I had a job. I had a job in the bakery, so I never eat, I never eat any in the mess hall. Galley they call it I guess. I eat fresh bread and pies the whole way back for 11 days from Japan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, if the war had continued, your company, was it the whole company that was on board ship?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: It was on 101.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: 101. And what were you guys responsible for? What were you --

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, we were just an infantry outfit is all. We wasn't specialized in anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You knew you were going right to Japan?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: No. We were -- well, when we left -- right away when we left, the war was still on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. And where were you headed, do you know even?

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Well, we went to the Philippines. That's where we were headed, I guess. But I figure if the war wouldn't have ended when it did, I might have been in the invasion in Japan, but that made me really feel good. It made me feel better after everything was over with and then since I've been home, since I've got time to think about it, that it's really amazing that I didn't make it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Make it there as an invasion fleet.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right. Okay. That's good. That's good. See how easy that was.

sp.speaker: Daniel Ash
sp.p: Okay. I hope it turns out all right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What I want you to do is, I want to get you -- I do want to get -- (DVD concluded.) - - -
